items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: We were all ex-Sy Oliver members, except Charlie Holmes, the alto sax man. Freddie William was on tenor, George Duvivier on bass and Wallace Bishop on drums.

ctx.x: I told Norman that, and then he says that Earle Howard was the head red cap at the Pennsylvannia railroad station and asked me why didn't get a job carrying bags. He told me that in a very polite way and I told him very politely that I didn't like to carry my own bags and had no eyes for carrying those of other people. Many New York musicians had done it, but for the time being, I figured to make it in the music game, even if there was not much on the rail for the lizard.

So on November 21st of '47, I went into the 845 Club in the Bronx with a small combo lead by Billie Kyle. We were all ex-Sy Oliver members, except Charlie Holmes, the alto sax man. Freddie William was on tenor, George Duvivier on bass and Wallace Bishop on drums. The 845 Club was the only Negro night club in the Bronx

which was not very famous as a night club district but this club did a very good business. The featured, at different times were: Derby Wilson, a fine tap dancer on the Bojangle side, June Richmond who had gone back to her singing act after she left Andy Kirk, Willie Bryant, who was the perm ent Master of Ceremonies, Jackie Mabley, the woman comedian and George Kirby, an imitator of voices. A relief trio was lead by an organist named Lawrence "88" Keys. There was also a chorus line of six girls.
